prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

The plate is headed "check-source", with the standing line "Decides whether a historical PDF's own text can be trusted, or which rescue source to use, and records the verdict." beneath it.

The dominant picture, filling roughly half the page, shows One scanned book PDF lies open in a fanned stack of pages. A tag tied to its spine reads year, author and title. A counter beside it shows the page count. Five slender bookmark probes rise from pages at the start, one tenth in, one quarter, halfway and three quarters. Each probe lifts a strip of text toward a four-step gauge marked high, medium, low and none. From the gauge, the path forks. High or medium goes straight on as trusted text. Low or none turns aside toward the online libraries in . Both routes converge on a single record card in . Arrows run one way, from book to gauge to fork to card.

Magnified circles set beside it show , first circle: a page with fewer than fifty characters is rejected. Second circle: a page crowded with symbols falls below six in ten letters. Third circle: a page of real prose passes with at least ten words. , first study: an Internet Archive shelf is searched by the first six title words, with a half-the-words title match. Second study: a Project Gutenberg shelf, reached only when the Archive finds nothing. A gate marked --skip-online bars both.

Colour is used so that Green means a page or text layer that passed. Rust means failed text needing OCR. Blue means the online rescue path and its source URL.

Draw these quantities as dimension marks or counts: up to 5 sample pages; grade thresholds 0.7 for high and 0.3 for medium; 50 characters, six in ten letters, and 10 words per passing page; first 6 title words searched; 2 online libraries tried in order; 4 verdicts.

These trade words appear on the plate, each set against the thing it names: check-source on the title. .meta.yaml on the record card, inside its check-source folder. source_type, source URL and difficulty on the card's fields. extract-text on the arrow leaving the card. text quality with high, medium, low and none on the gauge. --skip-online on the gate before the libraries. Internet Archive and Project Gutenberg on the two shelves. embedded, archive, gutenberg and ocr-needed on the four verdict tokens along the foot. The difficulty grades beneath the tokens are easy under embedded, archive and gutenberg; medium also possible under embedded; hard under ocr-needed.

Letter these words onto the drawings, spelled exactly as given: Year, Author, Title; page count; page 1; one tenth in; one quarter; halfway; three quarters; text quality; high; medium; low; none at least 50 characters; six in ten letters; ten words or more Internet Archive; Project Gutenberg; title match; --skip-online .meta.yaml; source_type; source URL; difficulty; extract-text embedded; archive; gutenberg; ocr-needed

Set these short notes beside what they explain: Five pages sampled across the book; Grade set by share of passing pages Each page must pass all three tests Archive asked first, Gutenberg only if missed; Online edition replaces only failing text The next stage reads this file; Without a project folder, printed instead A good text layer always wins
